evidence.label: Universal Tensor Squares for Symmetric Groups
A Cyclic Polytabloid Proof of Saxl's Conjecture

headline: The staircase representation's tensor square contains every irreducible representation, proving Saxl's conjecture.
scope: The results are about symmetric groups and their complex representations. The tensor-square statement holds in every size except 2, 4 and 9, where it is false.
plain: The symmetric group shuffles n objects, and its basic building-block representations are labelled by partitions of n. Saxl conjectured in 2012 that the staircase partition's representation, multiplied by itself, contains every building block. Two papers prove this, with a Lean check. They also prove that, for every n except 2, 4 and 9, some building block's square contains all of them.
doesNot: This does not compute the multiplicities, called Kronecker coefficients; it only shows they are all positive.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Jan Saxl, UCLA Combinatorics Seminar (recorded by Pak, Panova and Vallejo)
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles Saxl's conjecture and the tensor square conjecture, both well-known problems in algebraic combinatorics, with a Lean check.

explanation:
Take the six shuffles of three objects, the symmetric group S₃. It has three irreducible representations, the building blocks that cannot be split further. They have dimensions 1, 1 and 2: the trivial one, the sign, and the standard one. Multiply the standard one by itself, a tensor square. Its dimension is 2 × 2 = 4. A character calculation shows it splits as 1 + 1 + 2. Every building block appears exactly once.

Try S₄, with 24 shuffles. Its building blocks have dimensions 1, 3, 2, 3 and 1. The only candidate with a chance is the two-dimensional one, for a reason explained below. Its square has dimension 4, and it splits as 1 + 1 + 2. Both three-dimensional blocks are missing. So for four objects no building block works.

Building blocks of the symmetric group on n objects are labelled by partitions of n: ways to write n as a decreasing sum. The standard block of S₃ is the partition 2 + 1, drawn as a staircase of rows 2 and 1. The number of times one block appears in the product of two others is a Kronecker coefficient. These numbers are notoriously hard to understand.

Saxl's conjecture is about staircases, with rows m, m − 1, down to 1. It says the square of the staircase block contains every building block. Jan Saxl proposed it at a UCLA seminar on 20 March 2012[2]. Much partial support existed. Ikenmeyer proved it for blocks comparable with the staircase in a natural order[3]. Luo and Sellke showed the square contains almost all blocks[8].

The cyclic polytabloid paper proves Saxl's conjecture for every staircase[1]. The proof works inside one explicitly generated piece of the square[12]. The S₃ example above is the case m = 2.

The universal tensor squares paper goes further. For every n except 2, 4 and 9, some building block has a square containing every building block[4,5]. Pak, Panova and Vallejo had stated this as the tensor square conjecture[7]. A working block must equal its own mirror image, the partition flipped across its diagonal[6]. That is why only the two-dimensional block of S₄ had a chance.

Staircases exist only when n is a triangle number, like 3, 6 or 10. The new task is to reach every other n[13]. The paper enlarges a staircase by matching additions to its first two rows and columns. The one obstacle is that added boxes can create terms that cancel[9]. Two separate tests show that the enlarged square still contains each target block. It reuses the stronger form of the staircase result[11]. An exact computer calculation checks every remaining size up to 64[10].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked both main statements. It confirms the staircase result for every m. It confirms that for every n except 2, 4 and 9 some block's square contains every block. The stronger claim about one explicitly generated piece is not included. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major. Lean checks both main statements; the stronger cyclic form is not checked. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: All the ways to shuffle n objects, combined by doing one shuffle after another.
A way for the group to act by matrices that cannot be split into smaller such actions.
A way to write n as a decreasing sum of positive whole numbers, drawn as rows of boxes.
A representation multiplied by itself, so the group acts on pairs at once.
How many times one building block appears inside the product of two others.
The partition with rows m, m − 1, down to 1.
A partition that looks the same after flipping it across its diagonal.
